examples.text: Démerde-toi

glosses: het redden, het klaar spelen

examples.text: Ma copine se démerde toujours pour avoir les meilleures places.
examples.translation: Mijn vriendin speelt het altijd klaar de beste plaatsen te krijgen.

glosses: Aider.

examples.text: Une putain d'idée ! Il paraît que vous êtes le crack des cracks, que vous avez démerdé des situations indémerdables pour la Company. Les DG successifs se refilent votre nom comme le Saint-Sacrement.

glosses: Se débrouiller.

examples.text: — Ce que je vous demande, dit Julien, c’est de me garder un mois, le temps que je fasse ce travail, et ensuite, je me démerderai.

Aucune bestiole n'arrive à être aussi con et aussi irresponsable avec ses petits, même les serpents qui les laissent se démerder dès la naissance leur donnent, génétiquement et géographiquement parlant, de quoi se démerder.

[…], tout le monde s'était gavé, il y avait gagné le nom de roi d'Aragon et un champagne à son effigie, il en avait encore deux caisses, avant que les Américains ne se démerdassent comme des Américains et fissent pourrir le filon.

glosses: Enlever la merde qui souille quelque chose ou quelqu’un.

examples.text:
Morange remarqua alors son pantalon, souillé d’excréments. Il recula en grognant.
– Oh, merde !
Il n’aurait su mieux dire, mais il rajouta :
– Compte pas sur moi pour ça, démerde-toi tout seul…

glosses: wenig innovativ, eher unprofessionell und ohne Plan vor sich hin arbeiten oder eine Aufgabe in Angriff nehmen

examples.text: Jetzt, wo ich krankgeschrieben bin, wurstele ich den ganzen Tag über nur so vor mich hin.
„Ich möchte sagen, es ist nicht der Fehler, daß zuviel organisiert wurde, sondern es wurde zuviel gewurstelt und zuwenig organisiert.“
„Mit der Geschwindigkeit einer Schnecke wurstelte der alte Steiner nun die Zigarettenpackung aus der Brusttasche seines schwarzen Sonntagsjacketts.“

glosses: To subsist; to succeed, survive, or manage, at least at a minimal level.

examples.text: Do you think they can get by on only one salary?
Good girls do bad things sometimes / But we get by with it / Good girls do bad things sometimes / But we get by with it

glosses: To direct or be in charge of.

examples.text: Even though Jack is a novice, he manages his team with great success.

Interlaken East station is jointly owned with the standard gauge Bern-Lötschberg-Simplon Railway from Bern and Thun and the Swiss Federal Railways metre-gauge Brünig line from Lucerne, but is managed and staffed by the Bernese Oberland group.

glosses: To handle or control (a situation, job).

examples.text: The government managed the inflation very poorly.

glosses: To handle with skill, wield (a tool, weapon etc.).

examples.text: It was so much his interest to manage his Protestant subjects.

The moſt vnruly, and the boldeſt boy,
 That euer warlike weapons menaged […].

glosses: To succeed at an attempt in spite of difficulty.

examples.text: He managed to climb the tower.

Old Applegate, in the stern, just set and looked at me, and Lord James, amidship, waved both arms and kept hollering for help. I took a couple of everlasting big strokes and managed to grab hold of the skiff's rail, close to the stern.

Congratulations on managing to use the phrase “preponderant criterion” in a chart (“On your marks”, November 9th). Was this the work of a kakorrhaphiophobic journalist set a challenge by his colleagues, or simply an example of glossolalia?

glosses: To succeed at an attempt in spite of difficulty.
To end up doing something that could or should have been avoided.

examples.text: She somehow managed to sit on the wet paint.
Despite that, Swindon should have been level in stoppage time, but Mathieu Baudry somehow managed to put a free header over the crossbar from point-blank range.

glosses: To achieve (something) without fuss, or without outside help.

examples.text: It's a tough job, but I'll manage.

Plastics are energy-rich substances, which is why many of them burn so readily. Any organism that could unlock and use that energy would do well in the Anthropocene. Terrestrial bacteria and fungi which can manage this trick are already familiar to experts in the field.

glosses: To manage to say; to say while fighting back embarrassment, laughter, etc.

examples.text: "That's nice, dear!", she managed.

glosses: To train (a horse) in the manège; to exercise in graceful or artful action.
To treat with care; to husband.

examples.text:
[She] […]manages her last half-crown with care,
And trudges to the Mall, on foot

glosses: To bring about; to contrive.

examples.text:
in a town of war,
Yet wild, the people's hearts brimful of fear,
To manage private and domestic quarrel,
In night, and on the court and guard of safety!

glosses: The act of managing or controlling something.

examples.text:
the winged God himſelfe
 Came riding on a Lion rauenous,
 Taught to obay the menage of that Elfe […].
Young men, in the conduct and manage of actions, embrace more than they can hold.
the unlucky manage of this fatal brawl

glosses: Manège.

examples.text: You must draw [the horse] in his career with his manage, and turn, doing the corvetto, leaping &c..

glosses: To handle verbally or in some form of artistic expression; to address or discuss as a subject.

examples.text: This book deals with incest.
With the return to monthly publication it is our intention to extend the variety of subjects dealt with, and it will also be possible to attain greater topicality.

glosses: To take action with respect to (someone or something).

examples.text: The treasurer deals with financial matters.
The teacher knew how to deal with these lazy students.

British Railways are beginning to reap the advantages of electronics applied to accounting. At Swindon Works, a computor, the first of its type to be used anywhere in the world, was installed recently to deal with the pay of some 10,000 employees.
Work on anti-frost precautions on diesel locomotives is to be speeded up to ensure that most if not all locomotives have been dealt with before the winter sets in.
It is therefore dealing with pollution in two ways—suppression and mitigation.

glosses: To consider, as an example.

examples.text: Let us deal with the case of China.

glosses: To confront or overcome any difficulties presented by.

examples.text: We had to deal with having just a gallon of gas.
She's dealing with a lot of personal problems right now.
Thankfully he'd dealt with such issues before, so he had all the necessary experience.

glosses: To be in charge of, act on, or dispose of.

examples.text: I can deal with this crew of workers.

glosses: To behave in a certain way towards.

examples.text: He deals fairly with his employees.

And I will set my ielousie against thee, and they shall deale furiously with thee: they shall take away thy nose and thine eares, and thy remnant shall fall by the sword: they shall take thy sonnes and thy daughters, and thy residue shal be deuoured by the fire.

glosses: To clarify by reviewing mentally.

examples.text: It's a bit confused at the moment, I'll try to sort it out later.

glosses: To arrange.

examples.text: Could you call Dave and sort out a meeting for tomorrow?

glosses: To fix (a problem).

examples.text: The computer won't let me delete that file; could you sort it out?

glosses: To organise or separate into groups, as a collection of items, so as to make tidy.

examples.text: Could you sort out your wardrobe and put the clothes you no longer use in one pile to give away and another to throw away?

glosses: To separate from the remainder of a group; often construed with from.

examples.text: We need to sort out the problems we can solve from the ones we can't.
They've already sorted out the students in group A, so we just need to worry about groups B and C.

glosses: To take action to stop someone who has been causing trouble, often by physically attacking them.

examples.text: If you do that again, I'll soon sort you out.

Most of the babies and kids would be put to bed by one of the adults and left on their own. Every half an hour a bluecoat would walk around the aisles and if they heard crying from your chalet they would put your block and chalet number on a board to the right of the stage. The first few times I went to a proper church and saw the hymn order to the side of the pulpit I wondered why nobody was going to sort out those kids.

glosses: To provide (somebody) with a necessity, or a solution to a problem.

examples.text: Hey man, I want some weed. —I'll sort you out, mate.
We really need to sort Chris out with a girlfriend.

glosses: To discover, as by asking or investigating.

examples.text: I don't know who the twenty-first president of the United States was, but it should be very easy to find out.
"Why shouldn't somethin' new and wonderful lie in such a country? And why shouldn't we be the men to find it out?"

Somethin' happens when everybody finds out
See the vultures circling, dark clouds
I haven't booked, so I don't have a clue as to whether the service will be busy or not. Supposedly, reservations are compulsory, but I want to find out what would happen if you just turn up.

glosses: To discover or expose (someone) as disobedient, dishonest, etc.

examples.text: He had been fiddling the books for years, but finally he was found out.

glosses: To uncover a weakness in (someone).

examples.text: He may cope with the multiple choice questions, but the written exam will find him out.
If you don't try, you do not find it out.

glosses: To discover (something), as by perceiving or coming upon it.
To receive the consequences of one's actions.

examples.text: With the way he behaved, it's no wonder he found out.
